accuracy.evidence: Matches DfE National Curriculum (2013) Year 1 Measurement 'tell the time to the hour and half past the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times' and CCSS 1.MD.B.3 'tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks'. The lab moves the short hand 1/12 of a turn per long-hand turn, so at half past the hour hand sits exactly halfway between numbers; p2 range 1-10 and p3 range 1-11 keep answers between 2 and 12.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known Year 1 errors reported by NCETM: reading the long hand as the hour (step 2 prediction 'On the 3', challenge answer '12 o'clock'), calling half past 2 'half past 3' because the short hand is near 3 (challenge and its message 'It has just passed 2'), and thinking the short hand stays on the number at half past (step 4 prediction 'Right on the 4').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagclock is the only lab with a draggable analogue clock face whose two hands are geared together: dragging the minute hand round drives the hour hand, and children set targets like 'Make 2 o'clock' with a Check button. flagunit, flagbond, flagskip and flagbundle are number and measure labs with no turning dial, and the 30% shingle gate passed against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Step 1 shows one full minute-hand turn moving the short hand from 3 to 4, so the link between the hands is seen before it is named. Reading steps then show three random clocks to read, the Set step makes the child build 2 o'clock themselves, and the half-past step animates the long hand to 6 while the short hand slides to halfway, labelled 'half past 4: short hand halfway'.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions use tempting wrong options: 'The long hand goes all the way round once. What does the short hand do?' (Goes all the way round too), 'At 3 o'clock, where is the long hand?' (On the 3) and 'At half past 4, where is the short hand?' (Right on the 4 or Right on the 5). Each is answered by the animation straight after, with 'You predicted ... spot on' or a correction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge rotates o'clock and half-past clocks with shuffled answer buttons and six m= messages tied to the wrong pick, for example 'The long hand on 6 means half past. Read the hour from the short hand.' and 'The short hand takes 12 hours to go round. The long hand takes 1 hour.' A rule card (Long hand on 12: o'clock, on 6: half past) stays on the canvas.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences with the Year 1 words o'clock, half past, hour, long hand and short hand, under the 5-7 family limit in the validator. Lab prompts are one or two lines a parent can read aloud, and the adult side names the curriculum statements, explains why the hour hand drifts, and lists the long-hand-as-hour mistake.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph carries one idea: two hands, the long hand on 12 means o'clock, the long hand on 6 means half past, and the short hand moves on slowly. The family tip is a real routine (pick two times in the day, like 8 o'clock and half past 6, and find both hands on a real clock) and the content gate's filler patterns all passed.

mobile.evidence: Phone screenshots on iPhone 13 in light and dark themes show the full clock face with all 12 numerals readable, red hour and teal minute hands that stay distinct in dark mode, and large answer buttons for the young class. The hands can be dragged with a finger and also set with 'Short hand on' and 'Long hand back' buttons; the walk gate passed on phone and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) ran clean in both themes on desktop and phone. The canvas aria-label states the current time and where each hand points after every move, each drag has a labelled button alternative, feedback is read through the aria-live status line, and Challenge answers are real buttons in a labelled group.
